headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via Firecrawl’s broad web/API egress into Marker’s document-processing workflow; capability conflict is limited by Marker’s no-write/no-network profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Firecrawl ingests and emits web content via scrape/crawl/search APIs, and Marker is a document-processing agent that can consume that content. The pair lacks any documented provenance or isolation mechanism, so malicious page text could be treated as instructions when passed from A to B. This is not provably default-manual only, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Firecrawl output is fed into Marker without content provenance tagging, injection is plausible.
IF Marker treats extracted text as instructions or prompts, attacker-controlled web content can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Add a strict content/instruction separator before passing A output to B.
Strip or escape all prompt-like markup from scraped text.
Require a human review step for any web-derived instructions.
Use a denylist for tool directives in extracted content.
requires-engineering: add provenance metadata and parser hardening.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Firecrawl touches web content, structured data, screenshots, and API keys, and has broad network egress. Marker is documented as having no filesystem read/write and no network egress, which reduces but does not eliminate leakage risk if A forwards sensitive material into B’s outputs or logs. The shared-pipeline risk exists in default use when A feeds B.
conditions: IF Firecrawl processes API keys or screenshots and forwards them into Marker, sensitive data can appear in B outputs.
IF the operator stores A outputs in a shared workspace, leakage risk increases even though B itself is local-only.
mitigations: Redact secrets before handing A output to B.
Disable screenshot capture for sensitive jobs.
Keep A and B outputs in separate directories.
Review logs for accidental inclusion of API keys.
requires-engineering: add automated secret scanning between agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Firecrawl supports multiple instances and has broad network egress, while Marker explicitly cannot write the filesystem, modify git state, or use network/MCP. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely; the main overlap is read-only document flow. Uncertainty is low because Marker’s restricted profile blocks the usual shared-mutable-resource pathways.
conditions: IF Marker is wrapped by an external orchestrator that grants write access, conflict risk rises.
IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable directory through an unlisted wrapper, contention can occur.
mitigations: Keep Marker in read-only mode.
Avoid shared mutable workspaces.
Serialize any external writes through one orchestrator.
Document ownership of each output directory.
requires-engineering: add locking if a shared writable store is introduced.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Firecrawl can produce scraped facts and structured data, and Marker is a document-processing agent that may render or transform those outputs. Because no verification or provenance controls are documented, B may treat A’s output as authoritative. Marker’s lack of action-taking authority limits blast radius, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF Marker consumes Firecrawl output without validation, upstream hallucinations or scrape errors can propagate.
IF downstream users rely on B-generated documents as factual, the cascade becomes operationally significant.
mitigations: Add source citations to every extracted claim.
Require validation against the original URL before rendering.
Flag low-confidence extractions for review.
Separate raw scrape output from final documents.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware transformation rules.

E_compliance.rationale: Firecrawl touches API keys and web content and has broad network egress, while Marker is a local document-processing tool with no network egress or filesystem access. If regulated data such as EU PII or secrets is scraped by A and then processed by B, retention and residency obligations can diverge even though B itself is constrained. The pair lacks documented compliance controls, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF EU PII or secrets are processed by Firecrawl and stored in Marker outputs, retention policy mismatch is possible.
IF the operator routes regulated data through A’s hosted APIs, residency obligations may be triggered.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through Firecrawl.
Purge intermediate outputs after each run.
Keep a local-only path for sensitive documents.
Review vendor DPAs and retention terms.
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing for regulated data.
